92.title: Take and read
92.hook: in a Milan garden Augustine hears a child's voice say take and read, and his long restlessness ends (Confessions 8)
92.howItsDone: Augustine's conversion is remembered by Christians across the churches, and his line about the restless heart is one of the most quoted in Christian writing. Many Christians read a short passage of scripture each day, and some let one verse speak to them as he did.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Monica's tears, and a bishop's promise about the son of those tears. Your line was tears are not wasted. Did a small sign of love go out? Day ninety-two.

Everyone knows the feeling of being stuck between who you are and who you want to be. The habit you'll quit tomorrow. And then tomorrow. Milan, the summer of the year 386. Augustine is thirty-one, a successful teacher of speaking, with a career on the rise, and he is falling apart. He's become convinced that the faith his mother prayed for is true. But he can't make himself step into it. He writes that he was bound, not by iron chains, but by his own will. One afternoon, with his friend Alypius, in the garden of the house where they're staying, it all comes to a head. He gets up, goes off alone under a fig tree, throws himself down, and weeps. How long, he says. Tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now?
screen: `TOMORROW, AND TOMORROW.` → `A GARDEN IN MILAN.` → `UNDER A FIG TREE, WEEPING.`

segments.voice: Then, Augustine says, he heard a voice from a house next door, like a child's, chanting over and over: take up and read, take up and read. In Latin, tolle lege. He stops crying. He tries to think of any children's game that uses those words, and can't. So he takes it as a command. He remembers hearing of Antony, the desert monk, who once walked into church, heard a Gospel line read aloud, and took it as spoken to him. So Augustine hurries back to where Alypius is sitting, where he'd left a book of Paul's letters, snatches it up, opens it, and reads the first thing his eyes fall on. It's Romans thirteen. In the King James Bible: "not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying. But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He says he didn't want to read any further, and didn't need to. It was as if a light of peace flooded his heart, and the dark of doubt ran away. Alypius asks to see, reads the next line, about welcoming the one who is weak in faith, and takes it for himself. And the two of them go straight inside to tell Monica, who, he says, leapt for joy. Years later, Augustine began his Confessions with a line many Christians know by heart: God, you made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. That garden was where his restlessness met its rest. One caution Christians often add: this isn't a recipe for opening the Bible like a fortune cookie. Augustine's moment came after years of searching, reading, arguing and being prayed for.
screen: `A CHILD'S VOICE: TOLLE LEGE.` · `THE FIRST THING HIS EYES FALL ON.` · `PUT YE ON THE LORD JESUS CHRIST.` · `NOT A FORTUNE COOKIE.` · then, large: `OUR HEART IS RESTLESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a book at random and read one line. Any book nearby: a Bible if you have one, a novel, a poetry book, a cookbook. Sit, and breathe first, and let your restlessness be there. Then open the book anywhere, and read one sentence, slowly. Only one. Don't hunt for a better one. Read it again. Ask what it might have to say to you today, if anything. If nothing, that's fine; you've still stopped. If you pray, you can ask God to speak through what you read. The bell holds the time.
Take and read. Tolle lege: a child's voice in a garden in Milan, and one verse that ended years of restlessness.
Your line: our heart is restless. Today, when you feel the pull of tomorrow, tomorrow, ask the garden's question: why not now? Tomorrow, a rich man's son who preached to birds. Day ninety-two.

93.title: Francis and the birds
93.hook: a rich man's son gives it all away and preaches to the birds, who stay to listen (Little Flowers 16)
93.howItsDone: Saint Francis's feast day is October 4, and many Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches hold a blessing of the animals on or near it. His Canticle of the Creatures is sung as the hymn 'All Creatures of Our God and King'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, take and read: a child's voice in a Milan garden, and one verse. Your line was our heart is restless. Where did you ask, why not now? Day ninety-three.

Picture the town square in Assisi, a hill town in Italy, around the year 1206. A crowd has gathered in front of the bishop. A rich cloth merchant is furious with his son, Francis, who has been giving away the family's money and goods to rebuild a ruined chapel and to feed the poor. The father wants it all back. And Francis, in front of everyone, takes off his clothes, every piece, folds them, and hands them to his father. From now on, he says, I can say freely, our Father who art in heaven. The bishop wraps him in his own cloak. The party boy of Assisi walks out of town with nothing. And some years later, on a road in the Umbrian countryside, he stops, because the trees are full of birds.
screen: `A FATHER, A SON, A BISHOP.` → `HE HANDS BACK HIS CLOTHES.` → `TREES FULL OF BIRDS.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Little Flowers of Saint Francis, a collection written down about a century after his death, and earlier by his first biographer, Thomas of Celano. Francis tells his companions, wait for me here, I'm going to preach to my little sisters, the birds. And he walks into the field and talks to them. He tells them they owe God a lot of praise: for their feathers, for the freedom to fly anywhere, for rivers and springs to drink from, for food they never had to plant or harvest, echoing Jesus's words about the birds of the air. And the story says the birds stay. They open their beaks, stretch out their necks, bow their heads, and don't fly away until he blesses them. Then they rise and scatter in four directions, like a cross. Historians read the Little Flowers as memory mixed with loving legend, and nobody can say exactly what happened in that field. But the heart of it matches everything else we know about Francis. For him the whole world was family. Near the end of his life, sick and nearly blind, he wrote a song of praise in his own Italian dialect, one of the first great poems in the Italian language. It's called the Canticle of the Creatures, and it praises God for brother sun, and sister moon and the stars, brother wind, sister water, brother fire, and our sister, mother earth. At the very end, he even welcomes sister death. Francis's feast day is October fourth, and many churches bless animals on or near it. A pope in our own time took his name, and titled a letter about caring for the earth with the canticle's first words.
screen: `MY LITTLE SISTERS, THE BIRDS.` · `THE BIRDS STAY TO LISTEN.` · `MEMORY MIXED WITH LEGEND.` · `THE CANTICLE OF THE CREATURES.` · then, large: `BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch a bird for one minute. If you can, go to a window or step outside. Find a bird, any bird: a pigeon counts, a sparrow counts, a crow on a wire counts. If there are none, watch a tree, or the sky. Just watch. How it moves its head. How it lands. Don't name it or photograph it. Let it be your brother or sister for a minute. If you pray, you can praise God for it, the way Francis did. If you don't, just be glad it exists. The bell holds the time.
Francis and the birds. The rich man's son who gave everything back, and called every creature family.
Your line: brother sun, sister moon. Today, greet one part of creation as family: the sun on your face, the rain, the moon tonight. Tomorrow, a nun who laughed. Day ninety-three.

94.title: Teresa of Ávila
94.hook: a nun who laughed, founded convents on the road, and said prayer is friendship
94.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Teresa of Ávila's feast on October 15, and her books, especially The Interior Castle and The Way of Perfection, are read by Christians of many churches as guides to prayer. Discalced Carmelite nuns still live by her reform.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis and the birds, and a song for all creation. Your line was brother sun, sister moon. Which part of creation did you greet as family? Day ninety-four.

Spain, the 1570s. A covered wagon lurches along a muddy road in the rain, pulled by mules, packed with a few nuns, their bags, and a woman in her sixties who is running the whole operation. Her name is Teresa, from the walled city of Ávila. She's buying houses, dealing with lawyers and bishops, borrowing money, finding cooks, and opening one small convent after another, across the country. She's funny. She writes letters full of gossip and jokes and complaints about her health. And the thing she is famous for, in the middle of all this driving and deal-making, is prayer. Not solemn, faraway prayer. The kind you'd have with a friend over a kitchen table.
screen: `A WAGON IN THE RAIN.` → `RUNNING THE WHOLE OPERATION.` → `FAMOUS FOR PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Teresa was born in 1515 and entered a Carmelite convent at about twenty. And for almost twenty years, she says, prayer was a struggle. She was often ill. She was distracted. She couldn't wait for the hour of prayer to be over. Then, in her forties, something opened, and she spent the rest of her life trying to explain it. Her most famous description comes in the story of her own life, which she wrote because her confessors asked her to. Prayer, she says, is nothing else than close sharing between friends: taking time, often, to be alone with the one we know loves us. Friendship. That's her word for prayer. Not performance, not a list of requests. Time with a friend who happens to be God. Later she wrote a book called The Interior Castle, picturing the soul as a castle made of one clear crystal, with many rooms, and God living in the very center. Prayer is the door in. She reformed her order, founding houses where the nuns lived simply, and worked with a young friar who became Saint John of the Cross. She died in 1582. In 1970, the Catholic Church named her a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for everyone; she and Catherine of Siena were the first women given that title. And she laughed. People still tell a story, not found in her writings, of her tipping out of a cart into the mud and complaining to God, and hearing, this is how I treat my friends, and answering, then it's no wonder you have so few. Whether or not it happened, it sounds like someone who talked to God as a friend.
screen: `TWENTY YEARS OF STRUGGLE.` · `CLOSE SHARING BETWEEN FRIENDS.` · `A CASTLE OF CLEAR CRYSTAL.` · `NO WONDER YOU HAVE SO FEW.` · then, large: `PRAYER IS FRIENDSHIP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: talk to God like a friend today. Sit, and breathe. If you pray, try Teresa's way for two minutes: no formal words. Just tell God about today, the way you'd tell a close friend. What annoyed you. What made you laugh. What you're worried about. Then be quiet a moment, the way you'd let a friend answer. If you don't pray, try imagining sitting across from someone who knows you completely and likes you anyway. What would you tell them? The bell holds the time.
Teresa of Ávila. The traveling nun, reformer and Doctor of the Church who described prayer as close sharing between friends.

Your line: prayer is friendship. Today, at one ordinary moment, the car, the sink, the line at the store, talk to God, or to the quiet, like a friend. Tomorrow, a teenage peasant who led an army. Day ninety-four.

95.title: Joan of Arc
95.hook: a teenage peasant hears voices, leads an army, is burned at nineteen, and is declared innocent too late
95.tomorrow: Camp 2 close: the story you're in
95.howItsDone: Joan of Arc is honored as a saint by the Catholic Church, with a feast day on May 30, and as a patron saint of France. Christians of many churches admire her courage and her answers at her trial.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa of Ávila, in a wagon on a muddy road. Your line was prayer is friendship. Where did you talk like a friend? Day ninety-five.

Think about yourself at thirteen. What you worried about. What you thought you could do. Now go to a village called Domrémy, in eastern France, around the year 1425. France has been at war with England for generations, and much of the north is occupied. A peasant girl named Jeanne, Joan, can't read or write. She spins wool and helps in the fields. And she says that in her father's garden she began to hear voices, which she came to know as Saint Michael, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret. They tell her to be good and go to church. Then, over the next few years, they tell her something impossible: go to the king's heir, and help drive the English out.
screen: `YOU, AT THIRTEEN.` → `A GIRL IN DOMRÉMY.` → `VOICES IN THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: At seventeen, Joan talks her way past soldiers and nobles to Charles, the uncrowned heir, and somehow convinces him. She's given armor and a banner, and in the spring of 1429 she rides with the army to the besieged city of Orléans. Within days the siege is broken. That summer she stands beside Charles as he's crowned king at Reims. A year later she's captured, sold to the English, and put on trial at Rouen by a church court run by clergy loyal to the English side. The trial record survives, and it's astonishing. Learned men question an unlettered nineteen-year-old for weeks, trying to trap her. The most famous trap: do you know you are in God's grace? Say yes, and she's claiming a certainty no one can have. Say no, and she's confessing guilt. She answers, in effect: if I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me so. The court falls silent. They condemn her anyway. On the thirtieth of May, 1431, she's burned in the marketplace at Rouen, asking for a cross to be held before her eyes, and calling on the name of Jesus. Twenty-five years later a new church trial examined the case and declared the verdict null: she'd been innocent. Too late. In 1920 the Catholic Church named her a saint. What were her voices? People have explained them in many ways, and the sources can't settle it. You'll often see her quoted as saying, I am not afraid; I was born to do this. Historians can't find that line in the records. But her answers at the trial show the same thing. She wasn't afraid.
screen: `ORLÉANS, THEN REIMS.` · `NINETEEN, AGAINST LEARNED MEN.` · `IF I AM NOT, MAY GOD PUT ME THERE.` · `INNOCENT, TWENTY-FIVE YEARS LATE.` · then, large: `I AM NOT AFRAID.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by one true thing today. Sit, and breathe. Think of one thing you know is true, and that you've been quiet about because it's uncomfortable. That you were wrong. That something at work isn't fair. That you need help. That you love someone. Hold it. Notice where the fear sits in your body, and breathe into that spot. You don't have to be brave for a lifetime. Just for one sentence. If you pray, you can ask for courage. The bell holds the time.
Joan of Arc. The peasant girl who led an army, answered her judges, died at nineteen, and was declared innocent too late.
Your line: I am not afraid. Today, say your one true thing, calmly, to one person. Tomorrow, the last day of the stories, and a look back at all of them. Day ninety-five.

96.title: Camp 2 close: the story you're in
96.hook: parables, a birth, a road, a cross, an empty tomb, a church on the move
96.howItsDone: Christians retell these stories every year through the church calendar, from the annunciation and Christmas through Holy Week, Easter and Pentecost, and remember the saints on their feast days. Many churches read the Gospels and Acts in order across the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joan of Arc, nineteen, facing her judges. Your line was I am not afraid. Did you say your one true thing? Today, the last day of the stories. Day ninety-six.

Seventy-five days ago, we started telling stories. Think back. A farmer throwing seed on every kind of ground. A woman sweeping the whole house for one coin. A servant who buried his talent because he was afraid. A young woman in Nazareth saying, let it be. A feeding trough. Shepherds on the night shift. Fishermen told to try the other side of the boat. A short man up a tree. A king on a donkey. A towel and a basin. A rooster. A cross. A garden, and a name said kindly. Then a road to Emmaus, a charcoal fire, wind and flame, a jailer, a shipwreck, a letter full of names. And saints: a mother's tears, a garden in Milan, birds, a wagon in the rain, a girl in armor.
screen: `SEED, COIN, TALENT.` → `A TROUGH, A CROSS, A GARDEN.` → `A FIRE, A FLAME, A SHIPWRECK.`

segments.voice: Mark's Gospel, the shortest, begins like this, in the King James Bible: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The beginning. Gospel is the old English godspel, good news, translating the Greek euangelion. Christians have always told it first as a story, not a list of ideas: parables that turn things upside down, a birth in the wrong place, a road through Galilee, one last week in Jerusalem, a cross, and an empty tomb. And here's the thing about the book of Acts, where this camp has lived for weeks. It doesn't end. The last scene has Paul under house arrest in Rome for two whole years, welcoming everyone who came to him, teaching, as Luke puts it, with all confidence, no man forbidding him. And then Luke stops. We never read Paul's trial or his death in Acts. The story is left open, mid-sentence. Christians have long read that open ending as deliberate: the story keeps going. Through Stephen and Philip and Lydia, then Monica and Augustine, Francis, Teresa, Joan, and millions of names nobody wrote down. Christians say every life that takes it up becomes another page. That doesn't mean anyone here has to believe it. Some of you are on this path because it's your faith, some because it's someone else's you love, some just to understand. But you've walked the whole length of it now, from the sower to the shipwreck. You know the stories. And the next part of this path moves from stories to practices: how Christians actually pray, sing, rest and live it, day to day. Camp three begins tomorrow. You're in the story now.
screen: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOSPEL.` · `ACTS ENDS MID-SENTENCE.` · `ANOTHER PAGE, AND ANOTHER.` · `FROM STORIES TO PRACTICES.` · then, large: `YOU'RE IN THE STORY NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line of your own story. Sit, and breathe. Of all the stories in this camp, which one stayed with you? Don't think too hard: the first one that comes. Now ask where it touches your own life. Maybe you've been the lost coin. Maybe you're the one up the tree. Maybe you're on the road to Emmaus, sad, not recognizing something beside you. Find one sentence that says it. If you can, write it down now. If you pray, you can offer that sentence to God. The bell holds the time.
Camp two, closed. Parable, leaven, talent, annunciation, Magnificat, manger, baptism, disciple, the keys, transfiguration, hosanna, Pentecost, martyr, conversion, Gentile, epistle, agape, saint.
Your line: you're in the story now. Today, tell one person one of these stories, in your own words. Tomorrow, camp three opens with what prayer is. Day ninety-six.

97.title: What prayer is
97.hook: less about getting words right, more like talking and listening to someone who's already there
97.howItsDone: Christians pray alone and together: many use set prayers such as the Lord's Prayer and the prayers of their church's liturgy, many pray in their own words, and some wait in silence. Many pray at set times, such as morning, evening and before meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, camp two closed with seventy-five days of stories. Your line was you're in the story now. Which story did you tell? Today, camp three: the practices. Day ninety-seven.

Here's something surprising. Lots of people who'd never call themselves religious have prayed. In a hospital waiting room. On a plane in bad turbulence. Lying awake the night before the results come back. Please. Just, please. It comes out before anyone decides to say it. And lots of people who've gone to church their whole lives say prayer is the part they feel worst at. They worry they're doing it wrong: wrong words, wrong posture, wandering mind, nothing happening. For the next few weeks, this path turns from stories to practices, the things Christians actually do, day to day. And it starts with the most basic one of all. What is prayer, actually? Christians would say: less about getting the words right than you'd think.
screen: `PLEASE. JUST, PLEASE.` → `AM I DOING IT WRONG?` → `FROM STORIES TO PRACTICES.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Our English pray comes, through old French, from the Latin precari: to ask, to beg. And asking is part of it. But the Christian tradition keeps insisting prayer is bigger than a request line. It's talking and listening, to someone who, Christians say, is already there before you start. Listen to Jesus on it, in the Sermon on the Mount. He says don't pray to be seen. "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." A closet: a small, private room. And don't pile up words, he says, thinking you'll be heard because there are so many of them, "for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him." So why pray at all, if God already knows? Christians have given many answers, but a common one is this: prayer isn't about informing God. It's about being with him. That's the talking half. The listening half is just as old. In the Hebrew Bible, a boy named Samuel keeps hearing his name called in the night, and an old priest teaches him what to say: "Speak; for thy servant heareth." The prophet Elijah looks for God in a great wind, an earthquake and a fire, and finds him instead in a still small voice. Christians pray in many ways. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran Christians often use set prayers, words handed down for centuries. Many evangelical and Pentecostal Christians pray freely, in their own words. Quakers often wait together in silence. The next days will try several. But under all of them is one simple shape. Talk, then listen.
screen: `PRECARI: TO ASK.` · `ENTER INTO THY CLOSET.` · `SPEAK; FOR THY SERVANT HEARETH.` · `SET WORDS, OWN WORDS, SILENCE.` · then, large: `TALK, THEN LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one sentence, then stay quiet one minute. Sit, and let your breathing slow. If you pray, say one honest sentence to God, out loud or silently. Not a speech. Just one true thing: what you're grateful for, what you're afraid of, what you need. If you don't pray, say one honest sentence into the quiet. Then stop. Don't add a second sentence. Just listen. You may hear nothing but your own breath and the room. That's fine. Listening is the practice, not hearing. The bell holds the time.
Prayer. From the Latin for asking, and for Christians something wider: talking and listening to God. Camp three's first word.
Your line: talk, then listen. Today, in one conversation, with God or anyone, say your piece, then listen twice as long. Tomorrow, a simple shape for prayer. Day ninety-seven.

98.title: A simple pattern
98.hook: many Protestant churches teach adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication as a shape for prayer
98.howItsDone: Many Protestant, especially evangelical, churches teach ACTS (adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication) as a pattern for personal and group prayer. Churches with set liturgies follow a similar movement of praise, confession, thanks and intercession in their services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prayer: from the Latin for asking, and wider than asking. Your line was talk, then listen. How did the listening go? Fourteen weeks on the path. Day ninety-eight.

Blank-page panic. You sit down to write a birthday card, or a toast, or a hard email, and nothing comes. Then someone says: just do three things. Say what you love about them, tell one story, raise your glass. And suddenly it's easy. A shape helps. Lots of people feel exactly this way about prayer. They close their eyes, and the mind goes blank, or it goes straight to a shopping list: help me with this, fix that, please make this happen. So many Protestant churches, especially evangelical ones, teach a simple four-letter shape to hang a prayer on. It's easy to remember, because it spells the name of a book of the Bible we've just spent weeks in. A, C, T, S.
screen: `BLANK-PAGE PANIC.` → `JUST DO THREE THINGS.` → `A, C, T, S.`

segments.voice: A is for adoration. Before asking anything, you start with who God is, the way the Psalms do: "O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker." Not thanks for what God's done yet. Just wonder at who he is. C is for confession: being honest about where you've gone wrong. The first letter of John puts it simply: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins." Christians practice it differently. Catholics and Orthodox also have confession as a sacrament with a priest; many Protestants confess directly to God, alone or together in a service. T is for thanksgiving: naming what you're grateful for, specifically. And S is for supplication, an old word for asking, humbly, for yourself and for others. Paul packs almost the whole shape into one line to the church in Philippi: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." Be careful for nothing means don't be anxious about anything. Notice the order. Asking comes last. By the time you get there, you've already remembered who you're talking to, been honest, and said thank you, and the asking usually comes out different. Nobody knows exactly who first put these four letters together; it's a modern teaching tool, not a verse. But the shape is old. The Lord's Prayer itself starts with hallowed be thy name, and gets to daily bread only after. Churches with written liturgies follow a similar path every week. ACTS is just a way to carry it in your pocket.
screen: `A: ADORATION.` · `C: CONFESSION.` · `T: THANKSGIVING.` · `S: SUPPLICATION.` · then, large: `A SHAPE HELPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one sentence of each. Sit, and breathe. If you pray, go through the four letters slowly, one sentence each. Adoration: one thing about God that fills you with wonder. Confession: one honest thing you got wrong. Thanksgiving: one specific thing from today. Supplication: one thing you need, or someone else needs. Leave a little silence between each. If you don't pray, try the shape anyway: something that fills you with wonder, something you'd do differently, something you're grateful for, something you hope for. The bell holds the time.
ACTS. Adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication. This week: take and read, Francis, Teresa, Joan, the story you're in, prayer, and a shape.
Your line: a shape helps. Today, when your mind goes blank or goes straight to the shopping list, start with A and work your way to S. Tomorrow, a prayer said with the breath. Day ninety-eight.
